'''''Amorpha canescens''''', known as '''leadplant''', '''downy indigo bush''', '''prairie shoestring''', or '''buffalo bellows''', is a small, perennial semi-shrub in the pea family ([[Fabaceae]]), native to [[North America]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Casey|first=P. A.|date=2011|title=Plant Guide for leadplant (Amorpha canescens)|url=https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/kspmcpg10248.pdf|url-status=dead|website=|publisher=USDA-Natural Resources Conservation Service, Manhattan Plant Materials Center. Manhattan, Kansas.|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170212103559/https://www.nrcs.usda.gov/Internet/FSE_PLANTMATERIALS/publications/kspmcpg10248.pdf |archive-date=2017-02-12 }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last1=Slagle|first1=Malinda W.|last2=Hendrix|first2=Stephen D.|date=2009-10-01|title=Reproduction of Amorpha canescens (Fabaceae) and diversity of its bee community in a fragmented landscape|journal=Oecologia|language=en|volume=161|issue=4|pages=813–823|doi=10.1007/s00442-009-1429-3|pmid=19707794|issn=0029-8549|bibcode=2009Oecol.161..813S|s2cid=16683620}}</ref> It has very small purple flowers with yellow [[stamen]]s<ref name="gardner2">{{cite book|title=Tallgrass prairie restoration in the Midwestern and Eastern United States : A hands-on guide|date=2011|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-1-4419-7426-6|location=New York|pages=154–155|last1=Gardner|first1=Harold W.}}</ref> which are grouped in [[racemes]].<ref name="lbj2">{{NPIN|AMCA6|Amorpha canescens |access-date=2010-03-26}}</ref> Depending on location, the flowers bloom from late June through mid-September.<ref name=":2">Penskar, M.R. 2008. Special Plant Abstract for leadplant (Amorpha canescens). Michigan Natural Features Inventory, Lansing, MI. 4 pp.</ref><ref name="gardner2" /> The compound leaves of this plant appear leaden<ref name="lbj2" /> (the reason for the common name "leadplant"<ref name="gardner2" />) due to their dense hairiness. The roots can grow up to {{convert|5|m|abbr=on}} deep and can spread up to {{convert|1|m}} radially.<ref name=":1" /> This plant can be found growing in well-drained soils of prairies, bluffs, and open woodlands.<ref name="lbj2" />

==Description==
Typically between {{convert|0.3|–|1|m|abbr=on}} tall, leadplant can be identified by its small purple flowers grouped in long spikes and its grey-green leaflets that are alternate and pinnately compound.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lis|first1=Anna|last2=Adamczewska|first2=Anna|last3=Banaszczak|first3=Piotr|date=2014-01-01|title=Chemical Composition of the Essential Oil of Amorpha canescens Pursh|journal=Journal of Oleo Science|volume=63|issue=12|pages=1269–1274|doi=10.5650/jos.ess14152|pmid=25452264|doi-access=free}}</ref> The plant produces fruits in the form of hairy [[legume]]s each with one seed inside. The flower and leafing pattern is similar to ''[[Amorpha fruticosa]]'', however, ''A. canescens'' typically only grows to be {{convert|1|meter|sp=us}} high and prefers drier habitats whereas ''A. fruticosa'' can grow to be {{convert|5|or|6|meters|sp=us}} high and lives in wetter areas.

==Uses==
Leadplant is used for a variety of different purposes. [[Indigenous peoples of north america|Indigenous peoples]] such as the [[Oglala Lakota|Oglala]] use the plant for medicinal purposes.<ref name="herb.umd.umich.edu2">[http://herb.umd.umich.edu/herb/search.pl?searchstring=Amorpha+canescens Species account from Native American Ethnobotany (University of Michigan - Dearborn)] Retrieved 2010-03-26</ref><ref name=":0" /> Some indigenous tribes believed that the plant could aide in treating [[Pinworm infection|pinworms]], [[Dermatitis|eczema]], [[rheumatism]], neuralgia, open wounds, and cuts. The leaves of the plant were also used to make a tea and as a smoking mixture when dried, crushed and combined with [[American Bison|buffalo]] fat.<ref name="herb.umd.umich.edu2" /><ref>Gilmore MR (1919) Uses of plants by the Indians of the Missouri River Region. Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology, 33, 1-126.</ref> It also provides many benefits to the ecosystems it is a part of, for example it provides valuable nutrition for grazing animals and helps prevent soil erosion.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hickman|first1=Karen R.|last2=Hartnett|first2=David C.|date=2002-03-01|title=Effects of grazing intensity on growth, reproduction, and abundance of three palatable forbs in Kansas tallgrass prairie|journal=Plant Ecology|language=en|volume=159|issue=1|pages=23–33|doi=10.1023/A:1015534721939|bibcode=2002PlEco.159...23H |s2cid=23879535|issn=1385-0237}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Leadplant may also be used in landscaping and gardening purposes due to its [[nitrogen fixation |nitrogen fixing]] qualities and ability to help prevent erosion.<ref name=":3" /> Its nodulated roots are home to [[nitrogen fixing bacteria]] which help the plants grow.<ref name=":3" /> On the western side of the [[Mississippi River]] in [[Iowa]], [[Meskwaki]] women searched for the plant as it sometimes foretold the presence of [[lead]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Zimmer |first1=Eric |title=Red Earth Nation: A History of the Meskwaki Settlement |date=2024 |publisher=University of Oklahoma Press |page=42 |isbn=9780806195254}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Amorpha canescens'' was described by [[Frederick Pursh]] in 1814. It falls under subfamily Papilionoideae of the family [[Fabaceae]].<ref name=":2" /> The specific epithet "canescens" is a [[botanical Latin]] term meaning "becoming grey".<ref>[https://www.npwrc.usgs.gov/resource/plants/wildflwr/species/amorcane.htm NPWRC :: Leadplants (''Amorpha canescens'')] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100727045850/http://www.npwrc.usgs.gov/resource/plants/wildflwr/species/amorcane.htm|date=July 27, 2010}} Retrieved 2010-03-26.</ref> There have been further delineation beyond species of ''Amorpha canescens'' into distinct variants (such as the ''A. canescens var. glabrata'') based on the amount of hairs and color of the leaves, however this further distinction is not typically accepted due to the wide variation in pubescence of the plant.<ref name=":2" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Amorpha canescens'' can be found in many locations throughout North America, ranging from southern parts of Canada south to Texas and New Mexico and spanning west to Montana and east to Michigan.<ref name=":0" /> Leadplant is typically found in dry [[prairie]] and [[savanna]] communities<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.michigan.gov/dnr/0,4570,7-153-10370_12146_12211-36376--,00.html|title=DNR - Lead Plant or Prairie Shoestring (Amorpha canescens)|website=www.michigan.gov|language=en|access-date=2017-04-19}}</ref><ref name=":1" />  Leadplant prefers drier, well-drained soil of many different textures including sandy, gravely, and rocky soils.<ref name=":3">{{EOL|642105|Amorpha canescens |access-date=2017-04-19}}</ref> Finding leadplant indicates minimal livestock [[grazing]] and well-kept land that is not overgrown or that has experienced regular [[Controlled burn|fire]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gibson|first=David J.|date=1988-01-01|title=Regeneration and Fluctuation of Tallgrass Prairie Vegetation in Response to Burning Frequency|jstor=2996561|journal=Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club|volume=115|issue=1|pages=1–12|doi=10.2307/2996561}}</ref>
